meta.descriptionEn: On the morning of 24 November 1974, a young scientist almost stayed in camp to do paperwork. Instead he walked into a hot Ethiopian gully, and a tiny fragment of bone caught his eye. Within weeks, a team had recovered about 40% of a skeleton that was 3.2 million years old. She was small, she had a chimpanzee-sized brain, yet she walked upright. And a Beatles song gave her a name the whole world would learn. This documentary follows the hunt, the argument it ignited about how humans began, the fierce debate over her fate in museums, and the questions scientists are still asking fifty years later. Who was Lucy, and what did she really change?
meta.descriptionUr: 24 November 1974 ki subah Ethiopia ke garam registan mein ek naujawan scientist ko ek chhoti si haddi ka tukra nazar aaya. Kuch hi hafton mein ek 3.2 million saal purana dhancha saamne aa gaya. Woh chhoti thi, uska dimagh chimpanzee jaisa tha, lekin woh seedhi chalti thi. Ek Beatles ke gaane ne usay duniya bhar mein mashhoor naam diya. Is documentary mein dekhein ke Lucy kaise mili, usne insani irtiqa ke baare mein kya badla, aur 50 saal baad bhi scientists kin sawalon par behes kar rahe hain.
meta.metaDescription: How a bone fragment in an Ethiopian gully in 1974 revealed Lucy, a 3.2-million-year-old ancestor who walked upright, and why her story still divides scientists.

articleEn: On 24 November 1974, in Ethiopia's Afar Triangle near the Awash River, an ordinary day was beginning on a scorching plain. Donald Johanson, a paleoanthropologist at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History, had planned to update his field notes that morning. He dropped that plan. Instead he set off with graduate student Tom Gray for Locality 162, hoping to find bone fossils.

For two hours the two men searched the dry, muddy ground as the heat climbed. Then Johanson had a hunch and decided to look at the lower part of a small gully. Other workers had already checked that gully at least twice, and at first glance there was nothing there. But as he turned to leave, a fossil caught his eye. On the slope lay a piece of an arm bone, and close by was a fragment from the back of a small skull.

Whose bones were they? Those bones would become known as Lucy. Who was she? Did our ancestors learn to walk upright first, or did they first gain a big brain? And why was an ancient skeleton named after a Beatles song? This is where the whole story begins.

articleEn: To understand Lucy's story, we first need to understand an old debate. The question was simple: what was the first thing that set humans apart from other animals? When evolutionary theory emerged in the early nineteenth century, biologists accepted that humans were distantly related to all other species. But there were no transitional fossils at the time, so scientists had no links between humans and other animals. They assumed that our closest relatives were the great apes.

But what would the first change have been? They guessed that after the split, the first traits to appear would be those tied to intelligence, such as a large brain, tool use and complex language. In their view, changes linked to intelligence came first. One thing never entered their thinking: walking upright on two legs, or bipedality. It was not counted among the early traits at all.

Then, in 1924, Raymond Dart discovered the Taung child. Its skeleton looked bipedal, not chimp-like. Yet there was something strange: the skull had no room for a powerful brain. It seemed to walk upright but had a small brain, which did not fit the old idea. So had upright walking come first in the human story? The question stayed open, because there was not enough data to make sense of Dart's find.

Anthropologists could not agree. One possibility was that bipedality came first. Another was that intelligence came first. A third was that some other trait did. The question of what first separated proto-humans from their great ape relatives remained unresolved. Meanwhile, fossils of Australopithecus africanus kept turning up in South Africa between the 1920s and the 1940s.

Some modern research suggests that bipedalism began long before the australopithecines, among tree-dwelling primates. One claim holds that an upright spine and vertical body began 21.6 million years ago, in the Early Miocene, with Morotopithecus bishopi. But that is a later debate. In the 1970s, science needed evidence that could show what changed first. Where was that evidence hiding? On a hot plain in Ethiopia.

articleEn: In 1970, French geologist Maurice Taieb identified the Hadar Formation in the Afar Triangle as a site for paleoanthropology. He recognised that it could be a rich source of fossils and artifacts from human origins. Taieb set up the International Afar Research Expedition, known as the IARE, and invited three distinguished international scientists to join.

The first was Donald Johanson, an American paleoanthropologist and curator at the Cleveland Museum of Natural History, who became a co-director and later founded the Institute of Human Origins. The second was Yves Coppens, a French paleoanthropologist and professor at the Collège de France, who was the other co-director. The third was the British paleoanthropologist Mary Leakey. Seven more French and four American participants joined them. In the autumn of 1973 the team began surveying sites around Hadar. Another source says the IARE recovered hundreds of hominin specimens at Hadar between 1972 and 1977, a difference in dates worth noting.

Now to the Afar Triangle itself. It is a geological depression that borders Eritrea, Djibouti and the whole Afar Region of Ethiopia. It was formed by the Afar triple junction, part of East Africa's Great Rift Valley. Some paleontologists regard it as a cradle of human evolution. The climate is harsh. The lowlands are hot, dry and short on wind, and they are among the hottest places on Earth. At Dallol in the Danakil Depression, observations from 1960 to 1966 recorded a daily mean temperature of 30 °C in January and 39 °C in July. Danakil's annual rainfall averages only 100 to 200 mm.

The main source of water is the Awash River, but it dries up in the annual dry season. It finally ends in a chain of salty lakes, and along its banks a narrow green strip supports life. The region also holds Lake Assal, which lies 155 metres below sea level, the lowest point in all of Africa.

Now the story beneath the ground. Here the spreading ridges of the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden and the East African Rift meet, which is why it is called a triple junction. Compared with the Nubian plate, the Arabian plate is moving northeast at roughly 20 mm a year, and the Somalian plate eastward at roughly 5 mm a year. About 33 million years ago the Ethiopian Flood Basalts erupted and covered a large part of Ethiopia and Yemen with volcanic rock.

Besides Hadar, the Afar region has other important fossil sites, such as Dikika, Woranso-Mille and the Middle Awash. The oldest known hominins and examples of early human tool culture have been found here. So what was the team about to find in such a hot, volcanic, fractured land? The first big clue appeared in the form of a knee bone.

articleEn: In November 1973, near the end of the first field season, Johanson spotted a fossil. It was the upper end of a shinbone, slightly cut away at the front. The real surprise came next, because another bone lay close by: the lower end of a femur, or thigh bone. When Johanson fitted the two pieces together, they formed a knee joint.

The angle of that knee, catalogued as AL 129-1, clearly showed that it belonged to a hominin that walked upright. Think about it: a single knee angle revealed that this creature walked on two legs. This is what reading the story from bones means.

Then came the question of how old the fossil was. AL 129-1 was later dated to about 3.4 million years, far older than the other hominin fossils known at that time. Upright walking, then, had begun very early in the human story. The site is also interesting in itself. It was about 2.5 kilometres from where Lucy would later be found, but it lay about 60 metres below the rock layer that held Lucy's bones.

The find came at the end of the first field season, and it was a tremendous start for the International Afar Research Expedition, because the evidence pointed toward upright walking. The team returned the next year for a second field season, and Hadar's hot ground lay before them once again. This time they found hominin jaws. More evidence from Hadar was now emerging, not just a single knee.

At that time science was in the middle of a big debate. Had walking come first, or the big brain? A single knee carried weight in that debate, but one knee does not make a whole story. Scientists needed a skeleton with many bones from one body. In that search, the morning of 24 November 1974 arrived, when Johanson dropped his plan to update his field notes. What happened next? A small gully, a hot plain, and a discovery that would change how the world thought.

articleEn: On the morning of 24 November 1974, near the Awash River, Johanson had planned to update his field notes, but he dropped the plan. Graduate student Tom Gray took him away from the paperwork on a spur-of-the-moment survey. The destination was Locality 162. According to Johanson's later accounts, the two men spent two hours surveying the dry ground in the rising heat. Nothing special stood out on the dusty earth.

Then, on a hunch, Johanson decided to look at the bottom of a small gully. Interestingly, other workers had already looked at that gully at least twice, yet nothing had shown up. The two were just turning back when a fossil caught Johanson's eye. On the slope lay a piece of an arm bone. Another account says he saw a gleaming white bone out of the corner of his eye and immediately knew it was from a hominin.

Near that piece lay a fragment from the back of a skull, and about a metre away was part of a thigh bone. As they moved up the slope, more bones appeared: vertebrae, part of a pelvis, ribs and pieces of a jaw. So many bones in one place, and all probably from one hominin. Johanson was amazed to find so much of a skeleton together. They marked the spot and went back to camp, because the many pieces seemed to belong to a single hominin.

After noon, all members of the expedition returned to the gully. They divided the site into sections so the excavation and collection of bones could be done carefully. The work demanded great care, and in the end the whole excavation and collection took three weeks. Every fragment was a witness in its place.

That evening, the camp celebrated. A tape recorder played the Beatles' 1967 song Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds loudly, over and over. That same evening, fossil AL 288-1 was named Lucy. According to sources, the name was suggested by Pamela Alderman, a member of the expedition. In Ethiopia she is also called Dinkinesh, an Amharic word meaning "you are marvellous."

Over the next three weeks the team recovered several hundred bone pieces. Most importantly, no bone turned up twice, meaning no duplication. That confirmed the team's early estimate that all the pieces belonged to one individual, not several. In the end it was determined that 40 percent of a hominin skeleton had been found there. Lucy remains one of the most complete Pliocene hominin skeletons today.

But were these the bones of a male or a female? Looking at a complete pelvic bone and sacrum, Johanson judged that it was female. The reason was the width of the pelvic opening, which these bones showed. In this way an unknown creature gained a name and an identity. But what do Lucy's bones really tell us? Each of her bones held a secret, and now scientists had to read them.

articleEn: Now let's talk about Lucy's bones. She was very small, about 1.1 metres tall and about 29 kg in weight. Not every source gives the same figure: another report puts her height at 105 cm, and weight estimates range from 13 to 42 kg, though most studies fall between 25 and 37 kg. So Lucy was small even for her species. Her skull was small and chimpanzee-like, with a brain size reported at roughly 375 to 500 cubic centimetres.

Below the neck, though, the story was completely different. Her valgus knee shows that she normally walked upright. Her pelvis and leg bones worked much like those of modern humans, which shows her species walked upright. The first reconstruction of the pelvis made the ilium look ape-like, but that was wrong, because the pubic rami could not even be joined together. Tim White's later reconstruction showed a wide iliac flare. The pubic arch was over 90 degrees, like that of modern women. But the acetabulum was small and primitive. That is what makes Lucy special: some parts are human-like and others are still like older apes. She also had lordosis, a lumbar curve in her lower back, which is considered an important sign of habitual bipedalism.

Now look at an interesting number. In Lucy, the ratio of humerus (arm) length to femur (thigh) length is 84.6 percent. In modern humans it is 71.8 percent, and in common chimpanzees 97.8 percent. Lucy stands right in the middle. This could mean that A. afarensis's arms were getting shorter, its legs were getting longer, or both changes were happening together.

Now diet. The rib cage of A. afarensis was not like ours but conical, like that of non-human great apes. Such a rib cage makes room for a large belly and long intestines, which are needed to digest plant food. From this, a plant-based diet was inferred. Johanson's team also looked at her curved finger bones and concluded that she probably still spent time comfortably in trees. A 2016 study suggested that A. afarensis lived in trees at least partly. But the extent of this behaviour is still debated. Some experts believe these arm features may simply be ancient inheritance from the common ancestor of chimpanzees and humans.

Now, how old was Lucy? In 1974, Maurice Taieb and James Aronson tried the potassium-argon method, but problems arose. The rocks of the area had been altered by volcanic heating, datable crystals were very scarce, and Hadar had no pumice clasts at all. Then fieldwork stopped in the winters of 1976-1977. Work resumed thirteen years later, in 1990, and by then the more precise argon-argon technology was ready.

By 1992, Aronson and Robert Walter found two layers of volcanic ash. The older layer lay about 18 metres below the fossil, and the newer one only about one metre below. Argon-argon dating of these samples gave ages of 3.22 and 3.18 million years. So Lucy's age was settled at about 3.2 million years.

Then, in 1978, Johanson, Tim White and Yves Coppens placed hundreds of specimens from Hadar and Laetoli into a new species, Australopithecus afarensis. The name comes from Ethiopia's Afar Region. At first the team considered Lucy an early member of Australopithecus africanus, but more skulls changed their view. So the story of Lucy's bones and age became clear. But how did she become so famous? The answer lies in a museum in Cleveland and in a book.

articleEn: With the permission of Ethiopia's government, the bones from Hadar went to the Cleveland Museum of Natural History, and Donald Johanson himself took them to Ohio. There, anthropologist Claude Lovejoy stabilised the pieces and reconstructed the skeleton. Hundreds of small fragments slowly took the shape of a structure. In that museum Lucy drew great public attention. About nine years later, once fully assembled, she was sent back to Ethiopia.

But Lucy was not the only story. In 1975, Johanson's team found another astonishing treasure at Hadar, called AL 333 and known as the First Family. It holds teeth and bones from at least 13 individuals and is estimated to be about 3.2 million years old. In 1975 the team recovered 216 specimens there. The 13 individuals are thought to have lived at the same time, and there are very few signs of carnivore attacks on them. But they were not necessarily a family. In 1981 Aronson and Taieb proposed a flash flood, while Paul Pettitt offered a different theory in 2013.

Now the book that took Lucy into homes everywhere. Johanson and Maitland Edey wrote Lucy: The Beginnings of Humankind. It was the first popular book on the subject, and in 1982 it won the US National Book Award in Science. Lucy became a household name. The reason was clear: her pelvis and leg bones worked like those of modern humans, while her small brain was like a chimpanzee's. That combination startled everyone. It strengthened the idea that in human evolution walking came before a big brain, and it also supported Raymond Dart's theory that australopithecines walked upright.

Then, in 1992, work began in the same Awash Valley on another, more complete skeleton. It was a specimen of Ardipithecus, which people call Ardi. Ardi lived about 4.4 million years ago, well before Lucy. Like Lucy, she belonged to the journey from hominid to hominin. Excavating, preserving and analysing Ardi was very difficult and time-consuming, and the results were fully published in October 2009.

So did Lucy lose her importance? No. Later specimens helped scientists understand the size of the species and the differences between males and females. But a question stayed attached to Lucy's fame. How did this young woman die? And why did her bones go on a journey to America?

articleEn: So how did Lucy die? The truth is that her cause of death has never been settled. Her skeleton does not show the signs usually left by being hunted and then eaten by scavengers, so investigators have no clear answer. Only one carnivore tooth mark was found, on the left pubic bone. It is thought to date to around the time of death, but it is not necessarily the cause. Her third molars had erupted and were slightly worn, which led to the conclusion that she was fully mature, a young adult. Her vertebrae showed signs of degenerative disease, though not necessarily of old age.

Later research found something more. Lucy had a marked thoracic kyphosis in her back, diagnosed as Scheuermann's disease. It was probably caused by excessive load on the spine. The condition looks like that seen in modern humans, which suggests that her way of walking was fundamentally human-like. The real strain may have come from climbing trees.

Then, in 2016, researchers at the University of Texas at Austin proposed that Lucy probably died after falling from a tall tree. According to John Kappelman, her fractures resemble the humerus fractures that humans suffer in falls, so she must have fallen from a tree. But Donald Johanson and Tim White did not agree with this conclusion. Is there any solid argument against the theory? Yes: similar fractures are also found in the bones of antelope, elephants, giraffes and rhinos from the area. So the fracturing may not have happened before death but during fossilisation, which is called taphonomic bias. Lucy could also have died in an animal attack or a mudslide. The fact is that no single answer is accepted by everyone.

In 2007, a six-year tour of the original Lucy fossil in America began, called Lucy's Legacy: The Hidden Treasures of Ethiopia. It was organised by the Houston Museum of Natural Science and approved by Ethiopia's government and the US State Department. Some of the income went to modernising Ethiopia's museums. But controversy had already arisen. Experts such as Owen Lovejoy and Richard Leakey objected because of the fossils' fragile condition. Johanson also feared damage, but he thought the tour would raise awareness of human evolution research. The Smithsonian Institution and the Cleveland Museum of Natural History declined to host it, and other museums preferred to show casts.

In May 2013 the original fossils returned to Ethiopia. At the National Museum in Addis Ababa a plaster replica is displayed, and later exhibitions used casts. In August 2025, Lucy and Selam were taken to the Czech National Museum in Prague for a two-month exhibition. So in the end, what did Lucy change?

articleEn: So what did Lucy change? Her pelvis and legs showed that upright walking had begun before the big brain. By 2024, scientists agreed that Lucy's species was not the oldest human relative, and that several hominin species existed at that time. Her species walked and lived in grassy woodlands rather than the open savanna.

But many questions remain open. Was A. afarensis an ancestor of Homo? The 2.8-million-year-old LD 350-1 may support that idea, though some experts call it too derived. The classification of Australopithecus is still tangled. The lesson is that every new discovery tests old answers.

shorts.titleEn: The Gully Everyone Had Already Checked
shorts.text: جس gully کو پہلے دو بار چیک کیا جا چکا تھا، وہیں سے دنیا کا مشہور fossil کیسے نکلا؟ 24 November 1974، Ethiopia کا Afar Triangle۔ Donald Johanson اس صبح اپنے field notes update کرنا چاہتے تھے۔ مگر انہوں نے plan چھوڑ دیا۔ وہ graduate student Tom Gray کے ساتھ Locality 162 کی طرف نکلے۔ دو گھنٹے تک دونوں تپتے میدان میں زمین دیکھتے رہے۔ پھر Johanson کو ایک hunch ہوا۔ انہوں نے ایک چھوٹی gully کا نچلا حصہ دیکھا۔ شروع میں کچھ نظر نہیں آیا۔ دونوں واپس مڑنے لگے۔ تبھی ایک ٹکڑا ان کی نظر میں آ گیا۔ ڈھلوان پر arm bone کا ایک fragment پڑا تھا۔ اور اس کے قریب ایک اور ٹکڑا۔ آگے کیا ملا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Jis gully ko pehle do bar check kiya ja chuka tha, wahin se duniya ka mashhoor fossil kaise nikla? 24 November 1974, Ethiopia ka Afar Triangle. Donald Johanson is subah apne field notes update karna chahte thay. Magar unhon ne plan chhor diya. Woh graduate student Tom Gray ke sath Locality 162 ki taraf nikle. Do ghantay tak donon tapte maidan mein zameen dekhte rahe. Phir Johanson ko ek hunch hua. Unhon ne ek chhoti gully ka nichla hissa dekha. Shuru mein kuch nazar nahin aaya. Donon wapas murne lage. Tabhi ek tukra un ki nazar mein aa gaya. Dhalwan par arm bone ka ek fragment para tha. Aur is ke qareeb ek aur tukra. Aage kya mila? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 24 November 1974, Donald Johanson dropped his paperwork plan and searched a gully at Hadar, Ethiopia.
What he spotted on the slope would become one of the most famous fossils ever.

shorts.titleEn: The Knee That Proved Early Humans Walked Upright
shorts.text: ایک گھٹنے کے joint نے کیسے ثابت کیا کہ یہ مخلوق دو پیروں پر چلتی تھی؟ November 1973، پہلا field season ختم ہونے والا تھا۔ Donald Johanson کی نظر ایک fossil پر پڑی۔ یہ shinbone کا اوپری سرا تھا، جو سامنے سے ہلکا سا کٹا ہوا تھا۔ قریب ہی femur، یعنی ران کی ہڈی، کا نچلا سرا بھی ملا۔ Johanson نے دونوں ٹکڑے جوڑے۔ گھٹنے کا angle صاف بتا رہا تھا کہ یہ fossil، AL 129-1، سیدھا کھڑے ہو کر چلنے والے hominin کا ہے۔ بعد میں اس کی عمر تقریباً 3.4 million سال نکلی۔ یہ site اس مقام سے صرف 2.5 کلومیٹر دور تھی، جہاں ایک سال بعد کچھ اور ملنے والا تھا۔ وہ کیا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek ghutne ke joint ne kaise sabit kiya ke yeh makhlooq do pairon par chalti thi? November 1973, pehla field season khatam hone wala tha. Donald Johanson ki nazar ek fossil par padi. Yeh shinbone ka upri sira tha, jo samne se halka sa kata hua tha. Qareeb hi femur, yani ran ki haddi, ka nichla sira bhi mila. Johanson ne donon tukray jore. Ghutne ka angle saaf bata raha tha ke yeh fossil, AL 129-1, seedha khare ho kar chalne walay hominin ka hai. Baad mein is ki umar taqreeban 3.4 million saal nikli. Yeh site is maqam se sirf 2.5 kilometre door thi, jahan ek saal baad kuch aur milne wala tha. Woh kya tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
In November 1973, a shinbone and a thigh bone fitted together into a knee joint at Hadar.
Its angle showed an upright-walking hominin, dated to about 3.4 million years.

shorts.titleEn: What Happened to Lucy? Science Still Has No Answer
shorts.text: Lucy کی موت کیسے ہوئی؟ تقریباً 3.2 million سال بعد بھی کوئی نہیں جانتا۔ اس کی cause of death آج تک طے نہیں ہو سکی۔ ڈھانچے پر ایسے نشان نہیں ملے جو شکار ہونے اور scavengers کے کھانے سے بنتے ہیں۔ صرف ایک carnivore کے دانت کا نشان ملا، مگر ضروری نہیں کہ وہ موت کی وجہ ہو۔ پھر 2016 میں University of Texas at Austin کے researchers نے ایک theory دی کہ وہ ایک اونچے درخت سے گرنے سے مری۔ مگر Donald Johanson اور Tim White نے اس سے اتفاق نہیں کیا۔ کچھ experts کا ماننا ہے کہ یہ fossilisation سے بھی ہو سکتا ہے۔ تو سچ کیا ہے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Lucy ki maut kaise hui? Taqreeban 3.2 million saal baad bhi koi nahin janta. Is ki cause of death aaj tak tay nahin ho saki. Dhanchay par aise nishan nahin milay jo shikar hone aur scavengers ke khane se bante hain. Sirf ek carnivore ke daant ka nishan mila, magar zaroori nahin ke woh maut ki wajah ho. Phir 2016 mein University of Texas at Austin ke researchers ne ek theory di ke woh ek unchay darakht se girne se mari. Magar Donald Johanson aur Tim White ne is se ittefaq nahin kiya. Kuch experts ka manna hai ke yeh fossilisation se bhi ho sakta hai. To sach kya hai? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Lucy's cause of death has never been settled. A 2016 theory proposed a fall from a tree, but Johanson and White disagreed.
Some experts say the damage may come from fossilisation.
